segments.text: Finding the enemy is one part of the problem.
Realizing that the enemy has found you and reacting in time is another.
On the Rafale, that job is handled largely by SPECTRA, the aircraft's integrated self-protection system.
It brings together warning sensors and countermeasures capabilities designed to help the pilot identify threats and respond to them.
The Typhoon uses DASS, which performs a similar role through warning, electronic jamming, and other defensive measures.
On British aircraft, that also includes a towed decoy.
On paper, both systems are highly sophisticated.
The problem is that this is also one of the least transparent areas of any modern fighter.

Manufacturers talk publicly about general capabilities, but they don't release enough detail for us to reliably compare how SPECTRA and DASS would perform against every radar, missile, or air defense system.
So there simply isn't enough public information to declare one of them universally superior.
And more importantly, neither system makes an aircraft invulnerable.
In a real mission, survivability also depends on planning, intelligence, electronic support, and the specific threats present in that area.
When we move into ground attack, both fighters offer a very broad range of weapons.
On the British Typhoon, you have weapons such as Paveway 4, Brimstone, and the Storm Shadow cruise missile.
On the Rafale F3R, you have guided bombs, the AASM family, scalp, and the Talios targeting pod for target identification, tracking, and designation.
But the real difference isn't simply about who carries more weapons.
It's about what kind of mission those weapons allow the aircraft to perform.
Brimstone, for example, was developed to engage relatively small ground targets, including moving vehicles and armored targets.
That gives the Typhoon a very specific option for attacking mobile targets.
On the Rafale, Talios works together with guided weapons to locate, track, and designate targets accurately.
The F3R standard also expanded the use of AASM, including versions with terminal laser guidance.
When it comes to longer range strikes, though, there's an important similarity.
The British Storm Shadow and the French scalp belong to the same family of cruise missiles.
Both were developed to allow aircraft to strike pre-planned targets without having to fly as close to heavily defended areas.
So that capability is not exclusive to either side.
And that's why simply saying the Rafale is more versatile doesn't really settle this part of the comparison.
The upgraded Typhoon FGR4 also has access to a very broad arsenal.
The real difference appears when you put a specific mission on the table.
What's the target? Which weapon is available? And under what conditions is that weapon going to be used?
There is, however, one difference that becomes much clearer when we look at the two aircraft families as a whole.
The Rafale has an operational naval version. The Rafale M can operate from aircraft carriers.
There is no equivalent naval Typhoon in service.
So for a country that needs a carrier-based fighter, that difference stops being just a technical detail.
It becomes decisive.
Of course, in this comparison, we're using the Rafale C, which operates from land bases just like the Typhoon.
The Rafale family also has an anti-ship capability through Exocet.
But once again, we have to look at the specific configuration.
Just because a weapon has been integrated into the Rafale family doesn't mean every Rafale operated by every country necessarily has that capability.
It depends on the version, the integrations that were completed, and the package each country actually purchased.
